problems.stem: A teacher reports that an AI feedback tool cut her essay-grading time from six hours to ninety minutes and wants to adopt it. Which statement best justifies the decision as a defensible technology choice?
options: The ninety-minute time saving alone shows the tool improves the class.
The tool returns comments fast, so students will read them more often.
The saved time is reinvested in conferencing with the four students whose drafts the tool flagged as off-topic, a learning activity she could not run before.
The tool is the newest product the district licensed this year.
problems.explanation: A defensible choice names the learning activity the change enables, not just the labor saved. Time saved is only justification when it is connected to a specific instructional gain.

problems.stem: A colleague says, "This reading-recommendation app is just a tool, so any equity problems come from how teachers use it, not the app itself." What is the strongest reply?
options: Agree, because software cannot be biased on its own.
The app's recommendation model was trained on past borrowing data, so it can steer striving readers toward easier books regardless of teacher intent.
Agree, because the teacher chooses which students log in.
The app is fine because students enjoy using it.
problems.explanation: Tools embed design and data assumptions that shape outcomes independent of teacher use. A recommender trained on past borrowing data inherits and amplifies those patterns; the recommender-systems fairness literature documents exactly this feedback-loop bias, where yesterday's popular choices steer today's exposure (Wang et al., 2022, ACM TOIS survey on recommender fairness). Naming the built-in assumption is the AI-literacy move.

problems.stem: A teacher plans to let an AI chatbot generate and answer the comprehension questions for a novel unit so students can move faster. Which concern most directly belongs in her decision?
options: Whether the chatbot's interface matches the school color scheme.
Whether students enjoy chatting with the bot.
Whether generating and answering the questions removes the close-reading and inference practice that was the point of the unit.
Whether the bot can produce more questions than the teacher could.
problems.explanation: When AI takes over a task, name the student thinking it displaces. If the displaced work was the learning target, automating it defeats the lesson.

problems.stem: Two third-grade teachers must choose ONE tool for a fluency block: Tool A is a flashy new AI tutor with animated rewards and no stated learning objective, Tool B is a plain dashboard that flags which phonics patterns each student misses. Which decision and reason is most defensible?
options: Tool A, because its novelty will raise engagement on its own.
Tool B, because the flagged phonics patterns connect directly to the fluency objective and let the teacher target small-group instruction.
Tool A, because students will ask to use it again.
Either tool, since both are AI and the choice does not matter.
problems.explanation: The instructional purpose, here targeting specific phonics gaps, drives the choice. Novelty and engagement are not substitutes for a named learning purpose.
